If you're building in Florida, your permitting process just got faster, cheaper, and more predictable. 

Governor DeSantis signed HB 803 into law today, effective July 1, 2026. It's one of the most substantive pro-private-provider reforms Florida has passed in years.

Here's what changed:

📍Statewide uniform permit application: The Florida Building Commission must adopt a single application for all commercial and residential projects by July 1, 2027. Less AHJ-by-AHJ variation.

✅ Mandatory private provider registration at every jurisdiction: Local agencies must maintain a formal, electronic, no-cost registration system for private providers. Less friction getting approved to operate in new markets.

⚠️Guaranteed right to use a private provider: Fee owners and contractors can elect private plan review at any point in the process. That right is now explicit in statute.

💸 Commercial permit fee reductions: a minimum 25% reduction when a private provider handles either plan review or inspections. a minimum 50% reduction when a private provider handles both. Agencies that skip the reduction forfeit the ability to collect fees entirely.

🏛 Local plan review authority narrowed: Building departments can no longer review plan sets for building code compliance. Their scope is now limited to local ordinances, floodplain management, site review, and administrative matters.

⏰ 10-business-day completeness clock: Local officials must flag incomplete applications within 10 business days. The old 20-day window is gone.

If you're developing in Florida, this law is now one of your best tools. Knowing how to use it is another matter and that's where we come in!

The $1.5 Trillion Question: Why Permitting Delays Cost More Than Construction Delays

Before founding GreenLite with my co-founder James, we spent years in commercial real estate development watching otherwise sound projects lose momentum—not because of capital, construction, or demand, but because they disappeared into permitting. It’s the least visible risk in development, and often the most expensive. McKinsey estimates that between $1.1 and $1.5 trillion in infrastructure capital is currently stalled in federal permitting alone. Now, imagine the magnitude of stalled capital at the state and local levels. Not delayed by labor shortages. Not by material costs. Simply waiting for approvals.

At scale, permitting is no longer a background process—it’s a competitive lever. If your competitor takes twelve months to permit a project and you take four, you’re capturing eight months of quantifiable value they will never see. For retailers, you’re open for business in time for peak season while competitors are still resolving compliance comments and revising plans. In downturns, the operators who can remodel and reset their assets the fastest will protect revenues, royalties and rents while others stall. In periods of consolidation, the teams that can move permits predictably win the rollout race.

We’ve seen this firsthand. Teams like Dine Brands Global transformed permitting from a black box into a repeatable system—averaging 15–25 business days from submission to issuance across 45+ active projects, with zero stop-work orders. Its operational discipline applied to a problem the industry has historically accepted as unsolvable.

My view is simple: 2026 will be the year permitting becomes a strategic differentiator. The operators who’ve built permitting intelligence into their real estate strategy will outperform. Those still relying on 60-day placeholders will be explaining missed timelines to their leadership and boards. Construction delays are frustrating. Permitting delays are optional.

content:
Last week at Nexus Labs NexusCon I jumped into the discussion in the Owner/Vendor session, a room putting several hundred owners and operators and several hundred software and service vendors into one conversation. The question on the table was basically: now that AI has effectively erased the cost of building software, do owners still need vendors at all?

My case was that building software was never the real hurdle for this industry.

The evidence has been out there for decades in the form of open source software. There are building controls options like Bitpool and OpenRemote, WireGuard for networking and Wireshark for diagnostics. For almost a decade you could assemble a lot of the operations stack without paying a license fee, so why didn't every owner or operator jump on this?

They aren't engineering organizations, they are business and finance organizations, so they are not set up to manage and maintain software. It's easy enough for a building engineer to stand up a small app that does something useful, but is that app still running in a year? Does the next upgrade quietly change its behavior? Is anyone backing it up? Who gets the call when it breaks at 2am? And don't even get me started on SOC2 compliance. Making your own AI raises the bar even higher. Do you have observability? How do you ensure consistency with a probabilistic model? How do you handle model upgrades? Buildings are managed on decade timescales and software demands attention every week. Owners and operators aren't staffed for that because it has never been their core business.

So I don't think software-as-a-service is dead, just the software half. The as-a-service half, the part where a provider stands behind a result, is becoming the whole product. And the AI wave is amplifying this, because while AI can do a lot, it can't take on accountability. Someone still has to be responsible for the outcome, not just the output. You can see the shift in the wave of outcome-focused providers emerging across the built world and operations: at GreenLite we deliver permits and get paid against the results, Outcome launched last fall as an orchestration layer for CRE operations, and Crosby is doing the same thing to legal work by selling turnaround instead of billable hours.

So to answer the original question, owners still need vendors, but only vendors that are willing to own the results.

For the owners and operators who were in that room: if the software itself is nearly free, what would you actually pay for? Are you considering building your own teams in house to manage software at scale?

content:
AI can do almost anything but lately I've realized the one thing it can't, take responsibility.

At GreenLite we've been scaling up by moving some production tasks from people to AI and we are finding that people delegate to other humans without hesitation, but they delegate to AI very differently. Why? 

When I delegate work to a junior person, I’m ultimately liable for the work, but that junior person is accountable. They have something real at stake - a reputation, an employee review, a career. When I hand that same task to a model, my liability doesn’t change, but the accountability layer underneath is totally gone. The work moves downstream, but responsibility moves upstream. It concentrates on fewer people (me), who are now accountable for more output than what they produced themselves.

There is endless conversation about AI displacing work but almost none about AI displacing responsibility. This second bucket is the operational problem, it's why every company adopting Claude Code and Cursor is now stuck with a glut of PRs. Work can be redistributed, but responsibility can only be carried, and a model can't carry it. It can't be liable, can't lose a license, can't sit across from a customer and explain what went wrong.

Ultimately models can take on work, but they can't take responsibility.

Our answer has been to treat human-in-the-loop as permanent architecture, not a transition phase. AI absorbs the production work but credentialed professionals own the deliverable, with their name and their liability behind it. At GreenLite we use AI, but we're responsible for the outcome, not just the output.  

It's also changed how I evaluate AI vendors. I look through the lens of one question: are you responsible for the outcome, or am I? A vendor that ships output and keeps no responsibility isn't reducing my team's burden, just moving it somewhere else. My people might get more throughput, but that just incurs a bigger burden of responsibility.

I'd love to know. If you are deploying AI you've probably got a model for the value of productivity, but how are you pricing responsibility?

content:
For most of my career, the two-pizza team was the go-to org design. A two-pizza team is an agile team that you can feed with two pizzas, if you need to order more, your team is too big. Six or so engineers, a PM, a designer, running on two-week sprints with a continuous delivery of incremental fixes and a major release every sprint or two. There was an engineering lead per team, multiple teams rolling up to a director of engineering, and so on up the chart. It was the default because the two-pizza team was roughly the smallest unit that could carry a product surface end to end.

At GreenLite that unit is now one engineer - one slice of pizza. Not one engineer with AI assistance doing their old job faster, but one engineer operating at the throughput of a team. So we have reorganized around it.

An engineer and a fractional PM, paired, own a product or feature; one PM supports several of these pairs. A designer is a shared layer, providing UX direction at the outset and stepping in for judgment calls mid-flight. 

There's a passage in Manuel DeLanda's "War in the Age of Intelligent Machines" that keeps coming back to me. He traces how military organization evolved from the phalanx, a massed formation executing one commander's will, to the small autonomous squad, coordinated through communications and feedback loops rather than proximity. His argument was that the unit of organization was never really a leadership choice, but a function of how fast information could move through the system. When the feedback loops changed, the formation changed, whether the generals planned for it or not.

Scrum was a formation built for the feedback loops of 2005 and now the loops have changed.
I don't think we've found the end state. The pair model creates new questions I don't have answers to - career paths, redundancy when one person is the whole delivery unit, where judgment gets reviewed, how to manage at scale. But going back to the six-engineer team would feel like marching a phalanx into a war with drones.

Genuinely curious what other teams are doing here. As you've reorganized for AI, what did you land on, and what broke first?

content:
Last week I posted about the challenge of intake failure in building permitting, and how it is preventable. I decided to dig in a bit on the impact. What I found is the same missing document can cost almost nothing or six figures, depending on when you find out about it. 

Here's what I mean.

A drainage study identified before drawings go into production gets scoped and produced in parallel with the design work. It still costs the consultant's fee and some coordination, but it costs almost no schedule.

The same drainage study discovered at the intake counter means: scope a consultant, wait for the work, resubmit, and then go to the back of the review line.

In our portfolio, projects that fail intake average 76 days longer from submission to approval than projects that clear it. Harder projects fail intake more often, so that gap isn't a controlled experiment. But close to two months of extra schedule, and the carrying cost that comes with it, is a good indicator of the calendar impact for an intake failure. 

Those 76 days are where the six figures comes from. 76 days of delay isn't just a slipped schedule, it's an opening date that moves. A location doing $2M a year in revenue that opens 76 days late has roughly $400K of revenue pushed out past the plan. Add carrying costs on the capital already deployed and the number only grows. The drainage study costs the same in both scenarios. The six figures is the price of finding out about it at the building department counter instead of pre-submission.

I spent years in several other industries before ending up at GreenLite, and this pattern isn't unique to permitting. Late-discovered requirements are catastrophic everywhere, in construction, in software, in manufacturing. The cost of a requirement isn't the requirement, but the timing of the discovery.
Permitting just happens to be the place where the industry has accepted late discovery as normal.

content:
When I started at GreenLite I made the naive assumption that building code should be easily computable. The building code is already code: IBC Section 1006.2.1 is an if-then statement with a lookup table. Occupancy classification is a taxonomy. Allowable area is basic math.

So why isn't compliance checking fully automated? Why is it still a human reading a PDF?

It's not that nobody has tried, it just hasn't scaled. Singapore tried in the 90s with CORENET, ICC launched SMARTcodes in the 2000s, and a generation of rule-based BIM checkers followed Revit.

The reason: compliance is a join between two datasets, and neither one has a standard schema.

On the rules side: there is no such thing as "the" code. There's a model code, a state adoption of some vintage, a stack of local amendments, and a plans examiner's subjective interpretation on top. Our database at GreenLite tracks almost 1 million individual effective provisions across 12,000+ jurisdictions. And within a single code, rules apply differently based on the scope and scale of the project. "The code" is heterogeneous and variable.

On the drawings side: a drawing set is not a database, but a communication artifact. The information lives in graphic conventions, annotations, schedules, and the unstated context shared between the architect and the examiner. And the set isn't comprehensive - it points outward, to specs, structural calcs, geotech reports, energy models, product data, referenced standards. The examiner review is scattered across a dozen documents, which have conventional formats but no actual standards. Two firms can document the same building in entirely different ways.

Every previous attempt at automated code checking failed on the same assumption: that the inputs would be standardized. Standardized models, standardized rule formats, standardized submissions. Which meant the normalization work got pushed down to the end user, and no architect is going to restructure their drawings to match a checker's schema - the effort isn't worth the time savings.

So what's changed? It isn't that AI can finally "read the code." It's that the frontier moved. The problem was never encoding rules, but normalizing heterogeneous inputs and validating outputs. That's a problem current AI is actually suited for: extracting meaning from unstandardized drawings, resolving which of a million provisions applies, and doing it without demanding the industry restructure its documents first. Once the inputs are solved, compliance is calculable and deterministic. More importantly, it's easy to bring humans into the loop for judgement calls.

The open question I keep turning over: does AI finally make the industry standardize its data, because standardization suddenly pays? Or does it make standardization unnecessary, because the models tolerate the mess (at a cost of tokens)? I genuinely don't know. But I think the answer shapes what documentation, and plan review, look like a decade from now.

content:
I started architecture school in the 90s and the first thing I learned was pen-and-ink drafting: line weights, lettering, and erasing (sort-of). Then I was introduced to AutoCAD in my last years of undergrad with a digitizing tablet, massive PC, and a plotter down the hall. Even in that clunky form, one thing was obvious: drafting was going to die. Mistakes were reversible, revisions were practically free - digital trumped analog. 

Drafting used to be a career, with its own ladder: junior drafter, senior drafter, chief. Firms were organized around the drafting department: the principal sketched, the department produced. Thanks to AutoCAD the department disappeared, but the work didn't. It migrated upward - architects had to become their own drafters. 

Then something stranger happened: the productivity gains disappeared too. CAD made revisions nearly free, so clients asked for more of them and architects didn’t effectively monetize them. Drawing sets got bigger and documentation expectations inflated until they absorbed the entire dividend. The profession adopted the tool and captured almost none of the value.

Twenty years later, BIM followed a similar path. Major efficiency gains like automated take-offs and clash detection, but deliverable expectations got higher with LOD requirements written into contracts. Some roles disappeared, but new ones appeared like BIM manager, and once again the efficiency was handed to the client for free.

Twenty years later. AI. 

Two data points make a trend line. Here's what the pattern says about AI:

- The exposed layer isn't "the architect." It's the production work - documentation and compliance, exactly where drafting and BIM sat.
- The labor will migrate upward again, and a new coordination role will appear. The AI enablement/FDE is this cycle's BIM manager.
- The profession will give the gains away a third time, unless it changes how it sells. Firms that bill hours will watch AI compress their hours, while firms that sell outcomes keep the dividend.

The big question that I keep coming back to is how to sell outcomes as an architect. At GreenLite we have figured out how to pivot the permitting industry to sell outcomes - but it's easy to quantify ROI in days saved. It is a much bigger challenge to pivot how we sell architectural design. How do you quantify the impact of good design at a commercial scale?

content:
After seeing commercial permits go wrong at scale, I can tell you the failure almost never happens in one single moment. It moves through three stages that build on each other, and while the objections from the jurisdiction may be different project to project, almost every failure follows the same pattern. 

First, intake. Industry-wide, up to 40% of applications are rejected at first submission to the jurisdiction. This is just a check for completeness, before anyone even looks at the plans, and failure is usually for missing requirements that were published and knowable. By failing intake a project loses weeks before a reviewer ever sees the drawings.

Then, plan review. In the industry, projects that fail first plan review go through at least two or three correction rounds on average. At about three weeks for turn-around on each, plan review failure can add months. Some of those rounds are unavoidable because some codes are ambiguous and reviewer interpretations are subjective. But a meaningful share of them trace back to issues that were identifiable before the first submission ever went out the door, and the many of the rest are avoidable with a log of past objections. 

Then, compounding timelines. Each failure is unexpected and causes ripples. The AOR has other priorities and can't drop everything. Consultants get re-scoped.  Financing extends. Opening dates slip. From what we have seen across jurisdictions, the gap between projects that clear first intake and projects that don't is 76 versus 131 average days to approval. That is almost 2x the timeline from cascading failures. 

None of the three failure modes are mysterious once you lay them side by side. They repeat by jurisdiction, by project type, and by the DOB reviewer. These issues leave a visible trail on every project, but most teams aren't structured to collect any of it, which is why the industry keeps paying for the same errors year after year.

content:
BIM emerged while I was teaching design technology at Columbia University Graduate School of Architecture, Planning & Preservation and it created a paradigm shift from modeling geometric data to building data. The building model became a database with material properties, geometry and information in one record. The dream was that once buildings were machine-readable, everything downstream would follow - Automated quantity takeoffs, automated code checking, and facility management that inherited the design data.

Twenty-plus years later, BIM is the standard. The promise came true but it only went as far as the architect and engineer of record, and it has struggled to move downstream because we still exchange databases as pictures. The reality is at every boundary where the data would be invaluable the model gets flattened. Permitting … flattened to PDF. Out to bid … flattened to PDF. To the field, yup … PDF or printed. The most information-rich artifact in the entire process gets converted to the least information-rich format exactly when coordination needs to happen. At GreenLite we sit at one of those boundaries, and across hundreds of projects in hundreds of jurisdictions, the submission that arrives is always a flattened drawing set.

Why? You could blame file formats and compatibility, but that is too simple. The real reason is four fold.  
- Liability: a contract document has to capture a moment in time, and databases are mutable by design. 
- IP: the design is the architect's intellectual property, and handing over the full BIM model is like shipping your source code instead of the app. 
- Incentives: structuring data is work the designer pays for and someone else benefits from.
- The receiving side: most of the 20,000 permitting jurisdictions in this country are built to accept on paper or PDF, not an IFC or RVT.

Pushing harder to adopt standards and keep the model live across the whole chain has worked where a single authority could mandate it, like Singapore or the Nordics, but after twenty-five years we have to consider that it may never happen in a market this fragmented

Which is why the current moment is interesting - instead of convincing an entire industry to produce clean data, an AI model can create data from the messy format the industry already produces. A drawing set is more than geometry because the schedules, annotations, and material callouts all have the information of a database, just flattened into text. We've seen it work, and there is a growing agentic PDF to BIM market.

Reading the drawings solves the problem BIM has been focused on for years, but without breaking the industry. I don’t think that kills BIM, but starts to smooth that hard boundary on handoffs so that ultimately BIM adoption may be quicker. It will create more use cases for data downstream, and potentially drive demand for interoperability that has been lacking.

content:
Two successful models for public-private partnership in permitting reform

A frequent objection to Private Plan Review goes like this:

If American cities already don't have enough qualified reviewers, hiring them away from cities creates none. Move a reviewer from a city payroll to a private one and the country has exactly as many reviewers as before. Anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something.

But a realistic solution to permitting capacity doesn't hinge on ownership. Where the plan review capacity sits matters less than the outcome. Can we build a permitting process that is faster, more transparent, and more predictable?

One licensed reviewer paired with a knowledge graph and agents holding every prior comment, objection, and interpretation ever issued in a jurisdiction covers ground ten reviewers working from experience or institutional memory will never reach. That same licensed reviewer also has access to a brain of comments and objections from thousands of other jurisdictions.

The number of experts does not grow. The output does. Three things have to come together to get there: Licensed AEC expertise, years of historical permit data, and discipline and trade-specific agents built to read plan sets to evaluate local code hierarchies, prior comments, and previous objection data to pair that with the sound judgment of experts.

We call the result AI-native permit intelligence, and this core capability already delivers the outcomes of faster and more predictable permits via two primary channels.

The first is via private plan review, where the developer is the customer and state or local law provides the regulatory framework for licensed private entities to review in place of the local department. Public budgets aren't touched, so no appropriation is required.

A second channel is through building department services, where the city is the customer, the city retains the front-of-house applicant relationship, and back-of-house reviewer capacity gets added behind the city's own permit counter.
Both are public-private partnerships. The difference is where the AI-native plan review capacity sits, behind the city's permit counter or in a separate entity.

If you build in more than a few states, you have likely already worked inside one of these models.

Private plan review is not a new idea, and it might already be legal in your city or county.

In my last post I laid out the two models for adding plan review capacity. The objection I hear next is that both are fringe.

Statewide private plan review exists in a minority of states, which leads people to dismiss the whole idea as too limited in scope. County and municipal programs run all over the country. Prince George's County, Maryland. Fairfax County, Virginia. Placer County, California. Your jurisdiction might already allow this. About 20% of the country does.

Nor is this structure novel outside of building code compliance. Private engineers approve aircraft designs under FAA delegation. Private labs certify electrical product safety for OSHA. Private firms audit the financial statements of every public company in America.

Consider what the last one means. American public equity markets would not function if a government agency had to review compliance for every firm going public or staying public. The demand is too great and the throughput capacity is too finite. So we built a supervised private profession to do the compliance, and the result is the world’s most robust public equity markets.

Joe Lonsdale and Judge Glock made a case for the benefits of privatization in June, and Justin Lopas from Base Power Company pointed out privatization and standardization are the only way to keep pace with demand for electrical industrialization. I would augment their case by pointing out that a solution has already been widely fielded. With a credential and expertise shortage hitting both sides of the permit counter, a public-private partnership via PPR or Building Department Services is already a policy success story.

I arrived here the hard way. I started GreenLite in 2022 believing developers and cities both needed help, and built toward serving both. The business model took time to get right.

Plan review is an essential civic function. It makes our communities safer and more functional. content:
There are 50 states referencing the same ICC codes, and roughly as many versions of them in practice.

The ICC publishes a set of codes designed to give the construction industry a common framework. Structural design, fire safety, energy efficiency, plumbing, mechanical systems. The theory is that a developer, an architect, or a contractor should be able to work from a shared baseline regardless of where a project sits on the map.

The reality is that every jurisdiction amends the baseline, and the amendments are where the real work lives. California layers in seismic reinforcement, Gulf Coast states add hurricane provisions, New England raises snow load requirements, and most cities apply their own energy overlays and fire district rules on top of whatever the state has adopted. Adoption timing compounds this, because the ICC updates on a three-year cycle but states move at their own pace. Some AHJs are still working from the 2018 code while others have pushed to 2021 or 2024, which means two neighboring jurisdictions can cite the same code family and still be operating under materially different rules.

For a developer running one prototype across fifteen states, this fragmentation is the hidden cost of building at scale. Two identical restaurants, with identical drawings, will move through review differently because the code in Jurisdiction A is not the code in Jurisdiction B, even when both cite the IBC. 

None of this is a knock on the ICC or on local amendments, which exist for legitimate reasons tied to climate, geography, and risk. The framework has to flex to reflect where a building actually sits. What we should stop doing is pretending that adoption equals alignment, because the teams scaling multi-state programs well have already figured out that code compliance is a data problem before it is a design problem.

(Series 2/5): No city hires their way out of the permitting backlog:

In 2014, the International Code Council asked 3,850 building code officials across all 50 states a simple question. When do you plan to retire?

More than 80% said within fifteen years. The survey is now twelve years old.

Nearly half the respondents were between 55 and 64, and only about 3% were under 35. More than 30% expected to leave within five years, and that window closed in 2019.

The industry published this warning about itself, but nobody has re-built or prioritized the talent replacement pipeline.

Certifying a building official takes 8 to 10 years, while an electrical inspector takes five. Only 1,000 people worldwide hold the Master Code Professional credential, the highest in the field.

Newer data points the same direction. A 2024 survey of code officials in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic found 39% plan to retire by 2029, and more than half by 2034.

The reflex is to say cities need bigger budgets; but again, look at the math.

More than 19,500 unique municipal agencies review construction permits in this country. Roughly 18,000 are towns that are likely too small to staff a dedicated building department at any budget. Recent reports indicate that 50% of American cities aren’t able to balance their budgets. A reviewer is a salary, a vehicle, training, and a pension. In a budget constrained environment, if cities are struggling to bid for and staff the same credentialed people as private Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) firms, it’s likely that they’ll lose those auctions on compensation.

It’s crystal clear why no city in America hires its way out of a permit backlog. Not enough qualified people are not out there to hire.

(1/5) The Case for Public-Private Partnership: Reforming Permitting in America

Every conversation about permitting reform in America is having the wrong argument.

The argument pits government versus industry, public versus private, regulation versus growth. Pick a side and a think tank stands ready with talking points.

Meanwhile the constraint is staffing. There is not enough qualified expertise to review a growing development backlog.

In 2014, nearly half the code officials surveyed by the International Code Council were between 55 and 64. About 3% were under 35. Certifying a replacement takes 8 to 10 years, and nobody started.

At the same time, America decided to build housing, power, clean energy infrastructure, and compute simultaneously. All categories of development need approval from the same understaffed permit counter.

So demand keeps climbing while the pool of qualified reviewers keeps shrinking, and every project still funnels through the same counter no city agency has enough people to staff.

Over the next few weeks I am going to lay out the arithmetic and the answer.

The math first. Why no city in America hires its way out of a permit backlog, and why bigger budgets do not fix a shortage of people who do not exist.

Then the demand side. How every national ambition in this country runs through a plan reviewer with a full queue on their desk.

Then the answer, which is not what the debate assumes. The lever is not who owns the review. The lever is how many plans one qualified expert can process. Licensed expertise, years of structured, labeled permit data, and trade and discipline specific agents built to analyze plan sets raise throughput per reviewer, and throughput is the number that we as a country need to move. This is Permit Intelligence in action.

A framework for delivering this capacity already exists much more widely than the industry appreciates. Permit intelligence is a capability that can serve both developers and cities. Private Plan Review (PPR), or a "permitting fastlane" serves the developer directly at the developer's cost. Building Department Services (BDS) serve the city agencies directly, addressing the root cause of all of the cities' permitting backlog: diminished qualified review capacity at the same time as skyrocketing development demand. Nearly a quarter of American permit volume already works this way, a public-private partnership.

I have spent four years on this problem and got plenty wrong along the way.
If you're a developer or manage a development pipeline, start here. Ask your team how long your slowest jurisdiction takes. Then ask the jurisdiction how many reviewer positions they have open, or if they're particularly budget constrained, perhaps how many plan examiners or code officials they would hire if they could.

The answers point to the same solution, one a growing number of states have already adopted.

When I started at GreenLite I made the naive assumption that building code should be easily computable. The building code is already code: IBC Section 1006.2.1 is an if-then statement with a lookup table. Occupancy classification is a taxonomy. Allowable area is basic math.

So why isn't compliance checking fully automated? Why is it still a human reading a PDF?

It's not that nobody has tried, it just hasn't scaled. Singapore tried in the 90s with CORENET, ICC launched SMARTcodes in the 2000s, and a generation of rule-based BIM checkers followed Revit.

The reason: compliance is a join between two datasets, and neither one has a standard schema.

On the rules side: there is no such thing as "the" code. There's a model code, a state adoption of some vintage, a stack of local amendments, and a plans examiner's subjective interpretation on top. Our database at GreenLite tracks almost 1 million individual effective provisions across 12,000+ jurisdictions. And within a single code, rules apply differently based on the scope and scale of the project. "The code" is heterogeneous and variable.

On the drawings side: a drawing set is not a database, but a communication artifact. The information lives in graphic conventions, annotations, schedules, and the unstated context shared between the architect and the examiner. And the set isn't comprehensive - it points outward, to specs, structural calcs, geotech reports, energy models, product data, referenced standards. The examiner review is scattered across a dozen documents, which have conventional formats but no actual standards. Two firms can document the same building in entirely different ways.

Every previous attempt at automated code checking failed on the same assumption: that the inputs would be standardized. Standardized models, standardized rule formats, standardized submissions. Which meant the normalization work got pushed down to the end user, and no architect is going to restructure their drawings to match a checker's schema - the effort isn't worth the time savings.

So what's changed? It isn't that AI can finally "read the code." It's that the frontier moved. The problem was never encoding rules, but normalizing heterogeneous inputs and validating outputs. That's a problem current AI is actually suited for: extracting meaning from unstandardized drawings, resolving which of a million provisions applies, and doing it without demanding the industry restructure its documents first. Once the inputs are solved, compliance is calculable and deterministic. More importantly, it's easy to bring humans into the loop for judgement calls.

The open question I keep turning over: does AI finally make the industry standardize its data, because standardization suddenly pays? Or does it make standardization unnecessary, because the models tolerate the mess (at a cost of tokens)? I genuinely don't know. But I think the answer shapes what documentation, and plan review, look like a decade from now.

Lease terms are compressing. Tenant optionality is real. Presence is a choice, not a lease obligation. The passive ownership model was rational when the market answered the relationship question for you.

content:
Here's a thought experiment: What if Uber worked like commercial real estate?

You wouldn't request a ride directly. You'd call a broker, who would negotiate with a fleet manager, who would assign a driver based on vehicle availability - not your preferences. You'd sign a 3-year contract for a specific car. No switching. No upgrades. If the driver was rude or the AC was broken, you'd submit a service ticket and wait. There would be no rating system. No route optimization. No estimated arrival time. No way to know if your experience was good or bad relative to anyone else's.

Sounds absurd, right? This is essentially how CRE operates.

Brokers own the demand relationship. Property managers own building operations. Asset managers own financial outcomes. Marketing owns communication. Security own check-in. And there is no one in the CRE org who owns customer (B2B tenant) lifecycle and outcomes with any meaningful incentive, let alone the user (B2C individual) lifecycle and outcomes.

Uber didn't win because it had better cars than taxis (Black cars to start was cool, but small TAM). It won because it collapsed four layers of intermediation into a single, direct relationship with the rider by removing friction. That relationship generated data. That data enabled personalization and a better experience. That personalization created loyalty.

CRE has the same opportunity - and arguably a bigger one. Because unlike a 15-30 minute ride, a workplace relationship consumes more time. The data is richer. The touchpoints are substantial. The economic value of retention is massive.

But here's what most landlords miss: you can't personalize a relationship you don't have. You can't measure satisfaction for a customer you can't identify. You can't predict churn for a tenant you only talk to during leasing events.

The first step isn't technology. It's not an app or a platform.

The first step is deciding that the people in the building that make up a "tenant" are your customers - not just the name on the lease.

Uber figured this out 15 years ago. CRE is still debating it.

content:
Here's a number that should keep every landlord up at night: 39 points.

That's the gap in workplace experience scores between buildings that have earned Leesman+ certification and the average office building - measured across 1.5 million employees in over 10,000 workplaces globally.

To put that in context: imagine two restaurants on the same street. Same neighborhood, same price point. But one has a 4.8 rating on Google and the other has a 2.9. You'd never walk into the 2.9 unless you really, really had to. 
You'd assume something was fundamentally broken.

That's what's happening in CRE right now - except tenants can't see the ratings.

So what do Leesman+ buildings actually do differently?

It's not just nicer furniture or fancier lobbies. The data shows they dramatically outperform on the activities that drive retention and loyalty: collaboration, social interaction, learning from others, and sense of community. These are relationship outcomes, not design outcomes.

Meanwhile, the average office is losing the battle against the home. Home workplace satisfaction sits at 79.5 on the Leesman Index. The average office? 69.5. That 10-point gap has narrowed from where it was in 2019 (when offices averaged 64.3), which means landlords are investing - but most are still underwater against a competitor that doesn't charge the company rent.

Here's the uncomfortable part: 83% of employees say they want their workplace to provide a sense of community. And employees who like their workplace are 3x more likely to stay at their company.

Landlords who understand this have a direct line to their tenants' talent retention strategy. That's not a real estate conversation - that's a C-suite conversation. And it's worth dramatically more than the lease itself.

The 39-point gap isn't a quality problem. It's a relationship problem.

The buildings that score highest aren't just better designed. They're better known - by the people who operate them, and the people who use them.

When Spotify tells you it knows your listening habits better than your friends do, that's a relationship. When your building doesn't know if you exist, that's a gap. And it's 39 points wide.

content:
With the big commercial real estate service stocks all down, everyone is asking the same question: will AI kill the office?

While I, like everyone else, am concerned about AI's impact on knowledge work, I think the data (at least in the short term) is telling a different story. Here are the stats:
- San Francisco, the epicenter of AI, leasing hit 11.1M sqft in 2025, +59% YoY growth with AI firms dominating.
- Back in October, NYC office leasing hit a 23-year high.
- Trophy asset entered March hitting 95.5% peak-day (Tuesdays) occupancy according to Kastle, while office CMBS delinquencies reach highs at 12.3%.
- Only 7% of employees say they'd quit over a mandatory RTO policy, down from 51% a year ago according to MyPerfectResume suggesting The Great Resignation is becoming The Great Compliance.
- Team USA won hockey gold after a 46-year drought the same week office net absorption turned positive for the first time in years.

There are mixed signals in here for sure. With nearly $1B wall of office debt yet to mature and 49% of pre-2020 office leases yet to roll, every renewal is a referendum on whether the building deserves to exist in its current state. This is the REX Effect clearly playing out - a tale of two CRE's, the analogy legacy players vs. the experiential landlords. Mandates are a leading indicator with 12% more in-office time required, but attendance has only increased 1-3%. Mandates win the body but experience wins the mind. 

Another way to look at this bifurcation is the start of a new era - the "Presence Economy." As digital interaction becomes infinite and cheap, physical co-presence becomes scarce and premium. There will be an explosion of demand for people with skills to leverage AI, for sure. But there will also be an extreme premium for people with deep people skills - EQ, judgement, taste, etc. - all the things AI can only understand once humans define them.

The question for CRE is whether or not this will lead to a broader recovery of spaced lost over the past several years, an up-leveling of a smaller overall footprint, or some catastrophic collapse. What's your bet?

content:
Historically, CRE's customer has not been the tenant. Most operate like financial services firms. They sell an investment product to investors.

CRE also sometimes acts like they are unique in having investors and a fiduciary duty to them. But Disney, Marriott, AirBnB, Uber all have shareholders and fiduciary duty too. None of them treat the end-user journey as a nice-to-have. All of them treated it as the primary mechanism for delivering investor returns.

Disney designed the entire guest journey before they broke ground on a single attraction. Not the rides - the experience of moving through the park from parking lot to exit. They called it Imagineering. They built a science around knowing their customers called Guestology. Then they built a university to make sure every single employee understood their role in that journey.

Marriott built 271 million members not just by adding more points - but by building the relationship infrastructure that made every touchpoint smarter than the last.

Airbnb built an $80B company without owning a single building. Purely by owning the relationship.

CRE's old model wasn't wrong. When space was required for work and tenants had no alternatives, developing as a financial services product made sense. It's less true now now that the game is going to look like an operating business built for the end-user customer.

The operators winning today are winning on relationship infrastructure. The ability to know their tenants, anticipate their needs, deliver consistent value across the full lifecycle.That's not a technology upgrade. That's a structural shift in what the business actually is.

Disney answered that question in 1952. Marriott answered it with Bonvoy. Airbnb answered it with a thought experiment about surfboards and limousines.

CRE is being asked the same question now.

article.title: In CRE the tenant was never the customer. Now they have to be.
article.subtitle: Chase Garbarino
article.linkLabel: Open article: In CRE the tenant was never the customer. Now they have to be. by Chase Garbarino • 6 min read
article.description: Many of the major industries that went through the experience shift had one thing in common before it happened: they didn't reach the end user directl

content:
Many landlords I talk to say they want to be "experiential."  Very few can explain what that means operationally.

So here are three moves - that any portfolio can start executing this quarter.

1. Learn from Netflix's Onboarding (HqO Audiences feature)
When you sign up for Netflix, within 60 seconds you've picked your preferences, received personalized recommendations, and started watching something. The relationship is active before you've even finished your first session.

When a tenant moves into a building, what happens? Keys and a lease package. Maybe a welcome email. Then silence until something breaks.

The fix: Design a 30-day tenant onboarding sequence. Not a PDF welcome packet - a structured series of touchpoints that introduces the building's services, captures preferences, and creates at least one moment of unexpected value in the first week. Marriott does this with elite status perks on arrival. Your equivalent is making someone feel known before they've asked for anything.

2. Use Uber's Feedback Loop (HqO Feedback feature)
After every Uber ride: "How was your trip?" Five stars. Done. That single data point, collected billions of times, is the foundation of Uber's entire quality system.

Most landlords survey tenants once a year. Some never do. That's like Uber asking for a rating once every 300 rides.

The fix: Implement lightweight, continuous feedback at natural touchpoints - after a maintenance request is resolved, after an event, after the first month in a new space. You're not surveying people to death. You're building a Tenant Health Score from real signals, the way Uber builds a driver rating from real rides.

3. Steal Marriott Bonvoy's Memory (Make the Relationship Compound)
Bonvoy doesn't just reward loyalty — it remembers. Your room preferences, your floor preference, your pillow type. Every stay makes the next one better. The relationship compounds.

Most tenant relationships reset every interaction. The property manager who handled your last issue doesn't know about the three before it. The leasing team negotiating your renewal has no visibility into your daily experience.

The fix: Create a single tenant record that accumulates interaction history, engagement data, and satisfaction signals over time. When a tenant's renewal conversation starts, the leasing team should know more about that tenant's experience than the tenant does — not less (HqO CRM).

None of these require massive technology investments. They require a decision: to treat the tenant relationship as an asset worth managing, not just a contract worth renewing.

"Show me the incentive and I'll show you the behavior." Commercial Real Estate could use some of the late, great Charlie Munger's wisdom right now.

Who is the original customer of a commercial real estate asset? Frank Cottle and I discussed this on his excellent Future of Work podcast the other week.

Not the tenant. The investor.

The pension fund. The insurance company. The sovereign wealth fund allocating to real estate for yield, diversification, and inflation protection.

article.subtitle: Chase Garbarino
article.linkLabel: Open article: The Capital Problem in CRE by Chase Garbarino • 3 min read
article.description: This week's REX Effect is focused on exploring a conversation I had with Frank Cottle on his excellent Future of Work podcast. We talked a lot about t

content:
Why Doesn't Your Landlord Know Your Name?

Imagine opening Netflix and it has no idea what you've watched.
No recommendations. No "Continue Watching." No profile. You log in and get the same 8,000 titles as everyone else, organized alphabetically.

I've talked about this in past posts - The Urban Land Institute did a study revealing that fewer than 5% of employees can name their landlord. The company that owns the space where they spend a substantial amount of the hours in a week (yes I know some reading this are hybrid / remote).

In every other experience-driven industry, this would be considered a catastrophic failure of customer relationship management. At Netflix, if 95% of subscribers couldn't identify the service they were using, the board would fire the entire leadership team.

Maybe the reason employees don't know their landlord is because the landlord doesn't know them. In CRE, this is totally normal. And that's exactly the problem.

The commercial real estate industry has spent decades optimizing for one transaction - the lease. Sure all industries focus on their contracts with customers and accounts receivables from there. But in many other industries, and a growing number at that, there is a saying, "The sale starts when the contract is signed." This is the mantra that you need to win back your customer every day. And these industries have set up incredibly sophisticated operations to do just that. But CRE has almost no infrastructure for the customer relationship in between the lease signing and expiration outside of anecdotes.

Netflix doesn't just know your name. It knows what you watched at 2am on a Tuesday. It knows you paused on that documentary about whales. It uses every signal to make the next interaction better than the last.

Your landlord doesn't know if you use the lobby. Whether the elevator frustrates you. If you've ever set foot in the fitness center they spent $10M building. Whether you're happy, disengaged, or quietly planning your exit.

This isn't a technology gap. It's a structural one.

CRE has built an entire operating model around buildings without building an operating model around the people inside them.

That's what the Real Estate Experience gap is. And closing it starts with the simplest question any business should be able to answer:

Do you know who your customer is?

content:
Why Doesn't Your Landlord Know Your Name?

Imagine opening Netflix and it has no idea what you've watched.
No recommendations. No "Continue Watching." No profile. You log in and get the same 8,000 titles as everyone else, organized alphabetically.

I've talked about this in past posts - The Urban Land Institute did a study revealing that fewer than 5% of employees can name their landlord. The company that owns the space where they spend a substantial amount of the hours in a week (yes I know some reading this are hybrid / remote).

In every other experience-driven industry, this would be considered a catastrophic failure of customer relationship management. At Netflix, if 95% of subscribers couldn't identify the service they were using, the board would fire the entire leadership team.

Maybe the reason employees don't know their landlord is because the landlord doesn't know them. In CRE, this is totally normal. And that's exactly the problem.

The commercial real estate industry has spent decades optimizing for one transaction - the lease. Sure all industries focus on their contracts with customers and accounts receivables from there. But in many other industries, and a growing number at that, there is a saying, "The sale starts when the contract is signed." This is the mantra that you need to win back your customer every day. And these industries have set up incredibly sophisticated operations to do just that. But CRE has almost no infrastructure for the customer relationship in between the lease signing and expiration outside of anecdotes.

Netflix doesn't just know your name. It knows what you watched at 2am on a Tuesday. It knows you paused on that documentary about whales. It uses every signal to make the next interaction better than the last.

Your landlord doesn't know if you use the lobby. Whether the elevator frustrates you. If you've ever set foot in the fitness center they spent $10M building. Whether you're happy, disengaged, or quietly planning your exit.

This isn't a technology gap. It's a structural one.

CRE has built an entire operating model around buildings without building an operating model around the people inside them.

That's what the Real Estate Experience gap is. And closing it starts with the simplest question any business should be able to answer:

Do you know who your customer is?

That gap is where the opportunity sits.

The models keep getting better, and everyone can access the same ones. The model is not the edge. The edge is the data and business logic that the models can access. That is what makes AI dependable where the stakes are highest, and it compounds.

The firms that build that foundation now will be realizing real returns while everyone else is still verifying outputs.

Since getting started in 2014, our mission has been to give CRE investment teams the infrastructure to find the best deals, make faster decisions, maximize returns, and build a lasting competitive advantage.

Dealpath AI is the next step in that mission.

Drawing from your firm's own deals, comps, and institutional memory, Dealpath AI is built into the platform your team already relies on to accelerate every decision. 

From first look to IC approval, every decision your firm makes with Dealpath AI is grounded in how your firm actually thinks about deals. 

It starts with connecting your data directly to the tools your team uses every day:

💡 Dealpath MCP: Ask questions like "what's in due diligence?" or "draft a Q2 portfolio update" directly in Claude or ChatGPT, drawing answers from your live Dealpath data 

💡 AI Excel Assistant: Ground underwriting models in validated deal data and comps from Dealpath

💡 AI Listing Insights: Market context, tenants, and property highlights for every Connect listing at the point of deal entry 

💡 AI Deal Screening: Upload an OM, rent roll, T-12, or pro forma and get a full tear sheet in seconds, including deal highlights, BOE analysis, and portfolio fit insight

 💡 AI Comps: Relevant comps automatically surfaced from your proprietary database and MSCI RCA, attachable to a deal in one click 

💡  AI Extract: Structured data from OMs and flyers in seconds with 95% accuracy

Every deal screened. Every comp validated. Every assumption stored.

The firms building this foundation now will outpace the ones that start later. Not because of the model. Because of the institutional memory underneath it.

Proud of our team for everything they've poured into this. And grateful to our clients, whose trust and partnership made it possible.

We're just getting started.
